headline: The United States and 15 other countries are set to release a Kyoto statement that puts AI at the centre of a 'golden age of science'.
score_reason: A 16-country science declaration led by the White House is a real policy moment, but it is a non-binding vision statement reported ahead of release by one outlet.
importance_line: Scientists in 16 countries get a shared signal that AI-run labs and the study of how science itself works will shape future funding, while US research critics note the same administration is proposing to halve the National Science Foundation's budget, so words and money point in different directions.
summary: NBC News reports that the United States and 15 other countries, including Japan, Korea, the United Kingdom and the United Arab Emirates, will release the "Kyoto Vision for a Golden Age of Science" on Sunday at the Science and Technology in Society Forum in Kyoto, a statement led by White House science adviser Michael Kratsios that urges research built around AI (which it calls "super intelligence", following a recent executive order) and around metascience, the study of how science itself is done. Kratsios is expected to describe laboratories run by robots and AI designing experiments at superhuman speed, while Gretchen Goldman of the Union of Concerned Scientists said the administration's research cuts make its promises of trust hard to take seriously.
notes: Advance report; the statement is due the day of this edition. Could also sit in POL; kept RES per default and the curator's AI-for-science note.
